extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (with relevance to patent practitioners/applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and deciding patent claim eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the Alice/Mayo framework (including streamlined Pathway A), and for formulating and supporting §101 rejections. Covers identifying judicial exceptions, Step 2A/2B analyses, and when claims show self-evident eligibility or clear technological improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-of-use / technological environment limitations often non-meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: Many field of use limitations (and other non-meaningful claim limitations) are identifiable by an absence of integration into the claim as a whole and therefore do not add an inventive concept to the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples the courts have described as mere field-of-use/technological-environment limitations: limiting drug administration to a particular patient population (Mayo v. Prometheus); identifying participants as commodity providers/consumers (Bilski); narrowing a formula to a particular object (Flook); requiring execution in a computer environment or over the Internet (FairWarning; Intellectual Ventures; Ultramercial; buySAFE); limiting abstract ideas to power-grid data (Electric Power). Examiners should consider these limitations interchangeable with “technological environment” and consider overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (see MPEP § 2106.05(g)). When a limitation merely links use of a judicial exception to a technology/field, explain why it does not meaningfully limit the claim (e.g., employing well-known computer functions in a particular environment does not add significantly more).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: A data-gathering step limited to a particular data source or type may be both insignificant extra-solution activity and a field-of-use limitation and thus not meaningfully limit a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include limiting an abstract idea to the Internet or to power-grid data. Examiners should carefully consider each claim on its own merits and evaluate all relevant Step 2B considerations before making a determination on this consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) may be used when eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: For efficiency, examiners may use a streamlined analysis (Pathway A) when a claim’s eligibility is self-evident, e.g., because the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality. But if there is doubt, the full Alice/Mayo analysis should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The streamlined analysis yields the same result as the full analysis and is not a way to avoid a finding of ineligibility that would be reached by the full analysis. If eligibility is self-evident, the claim is eligible at Pathway A; the record may simply lack an eligibility rejection. If a claim is a “close call,” perform the full analysis (see BASCOM). Examples of self-evident eligibility: complex manufactured industrial products with meaningful limitations (robotic arm with control using mathematical relationships), artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral, claims that include only ancillary nature-based components (cellphone with gold contact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility is self-evident when claim does not tie up judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may bypass the full analysis if, viewed as a whole, it clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception such that others cannot practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that clearly improve technology or computer functionality (Enfish, McRO) or that clearly do not attempt to tie up a nature-based product may qualify. Only use streamlined analysis when eligibility is clear; otherwise use full Alice/Mayo analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear improvement to technology or computer functionality means not abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to clear improvements in technology or to computer functionality may not be abstract and thus may not require full eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples: Enfish (self-referential table) and McRO (automatic lip synchronization). If the claim clearly improves computer-related technology or other technologies/technological processes, its eligibility may be self-evident. But if it’s a close call (e.g., claims describing filtering content in BASCOM), perform the full Step 2B analysis to determine whether claims amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections must be based on substantive law and review the record as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rejections must be grounded in the substantive law under 35 U.S.C. 101 as interpreted by precedent. Examiners should review the record as a whole (specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law, prior art) before concluding eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training materials and examples explain policy but do not serve as an independent basis for rejection. The evaluation should be claim-by-claim; dependent claims may be eligible even if an independent claim is not. Examiners should be familiar with cited decisions and avoid relying on language taken out of context or on non-precedential decisions unless the facts uniquely match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case requirement when making an eligibility rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If more likely than not that a claim fails both criteria for eligibility (Step 1: NO and/or Step 2B: NO), examiners should formulate an appropriate rejection and set forth a prima facie case of ineligibility under substantive law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prima facie is a procedural tool allocating burdens between examiner and applicant: initial burden on examiner to clearly and specifically explain why a claim is ineligible so applicant has sufficient notice to respond effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: When making a §101 rejection, identify and explain why claim is not within a statutory category (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If claim is determined not to fall within a statutory category, the rejection should explain why the claim is not directed to one of the four statutory categories of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 706.03(a) for making such rejections and MPEP § 2106.03 for Step 1 discussion. The Office action must provide a sufficiently clear and specific explanation to enable effective applicant response.

rubrics_metrics.name: When making a Step 2A rejection, identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitations that recite or describe the judicial exception and explain why those limitations set forth an exception (e.g., an abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon, or product of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim describes but does not expressly set forth the exception, explain what subject matter is described and why it is an exception. When identifying an abstract idea, link it to concepts courts have identified as abstract (see MPEP §2106.04(a)(2)). Citing appropriate case law is a best practice. Avoid going beyond concepts similar to those courts identified and avoid non-precedential decisions unless facts match. Sample explanations provided: "The claim recites the steps of sorting information by X, which is an abstract idea similar to..." For laws of nature/natural phenomena: explain with reasoned rationale why the recited correlation or phenomenon is a law of nature or natural phenomenon. For products of nature: explain why the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart and use the markedly-different-characteristics analysis (MPEP §2106.04(b)/(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: When making a Step 2B rejection, identify additional claim elements and explain why they do not add significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception, point out additional elements beyond the exception and explain why those elements, individually and as a combination, do not result in the claim as a whole amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address the combination of additional elements because a new combination of known steps may be patent eligible (Diamond v. Diehr). Explain why particular claim elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities in the relevant art; provide a reasoned explanation supporting that conclusion. See MPEP §2106.05 for considerations courts have found to qualify or not qualify as significantly more. If additional elements provide an inventive concept, explain why they add a meaningful limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners should explain rationale and make rejections readily apparent from examiner expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner, relying on the examiner’s expertise in the art, in the Step 2B inquiry that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. The examiner must explain the rationale underlying the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explanation should be detailed enough for the applicant to effectively respond. Conversely, when appropriate, explain why additional elements provide an inventive concept by adding meaningful limitations (see MPEP §2106.05 and §2106.07(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply analysis on a claim-by-claim basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate eligibility on each claim separately because dependent claims may add limitations that render them eligible even if the independent claim is ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims do not automatically rise or fall with similar claims in an application; consider the particular elements recited in each claim when evaluating eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Under compact prosecution, complete examination under all other patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a §101 rejection is made, a complete examination should be made for every claim under the other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship and double patenting) and non-statutory double patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional when asserted
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding that particular claim limitations are well understood, routine, conventional activities, the rejection should explain why the courts or those in the relevant field would recognize those elements as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a reasoned explanation that supports the conclusion; do not merely assert routine/conventional status without evidentiary or reasoned support. This explanation applies both to individual elements and to their combination when assessing whether claims amount to significantly more.
